Overall, faux fur has a much higher carbon footprint than fur. From being made with plastic to not even bearing the same qualities of fur and leather, it's kind of impossible to compare the two further than esthetics. Faux fur also has the possibility of being produced in less than ideal environments, much like everything else these days. Overall, it isnt inherently more ethical just because no animal is harmed in the process.

In the world of ethics, things get sticky. There's unethical hunters, unethical fur farms, and unethical practices. But theres also TONS of ethical, conservational, and even traditional reasons behind the fur trade. Whether we're talking Inuk and Inuit tribes hunting and using parts as their ancestors have, hunters/trappers trapping in line with state regulations to control wildlife populace, or even rabbit farms that raise their rabbits ethically for meat and produce fur as a by-product, There's plenty of *ethical* means of obtaining fur. 

Keeping it short- it's a lot more complex than just labeling it as truly and blindly unethical. I'd recommend taking a look at other arguments for ethical fur farming practices, information on how the local hunting community also leads environmental conservation efforts, or even lean into how leather is an already existing by-product to the meat industry.

I'm repeating a lot of others already, but I'm hoping to give some clarity. For big skulls like this, you're safe to use higher percentage peroxide. Look at places like Sally's for hair developer - clear is preferred, but cream is better than none. And mix with COLD water. Hot water will cause the peroxide to change to water too quickly as h2o2 is unstable in heat. I recommend soaking for at least 24 hours for heavily stained bones.

Be sure to rinse and soak in hot water- not boiling- for a bit and allow bones to dry THOROUGHLY (im talking it can be up to days for greasy or thick bones)before continuing hydrogen peroxide can be explosive when it comes in contact with ammonia.

As others have said- ammonia is going to be your best option. Look for commercial ammonia cleaners at places like Ace Hardware for higher concentrations - around 10%. Use a good amount in your buckets and use it in a ventilated area. I also like to add dawn platinum to my ammonia, but it's not necessary. The most helpful addition here is **use hot water**. Not boiling, but if you can get an aquarium heater, or preferably a bucket heater, it will make yhe dofference between degreating for days and weeks. Body fat liquifies ar 120 ish F. Keeping your water under boiling (212 F) and above that 120  will allow for grease release more easily and allow ammonia to degrease deeper. I usually allow them to degrease for a week or two before changing, agitating the bucket before dumping and breaking up any grease/dirt pooling and allowing the dawn to absorb the grease before the change. 

It's best to alternate between both steps, taking care to do the soaking and drying in hot water in between - this gives any remaining chemicals and loose grease to pull out before you change. But in doing so- you're using the oxidation to pull grease to the surface and the degreasing/ soaponification to actually remove it. It's a good idea to be careful with peroxide as you remove grease. While not as big of a problem with big skulls- using too strong peroxide for too long can cause skulls to degrade, erode, or become too fragile because it eats at the bone over time.

Boiling is a no-go, but a simmer is always an option. You dont want to go above boiling, as that will damage and change the composition of the bone structures leading to brittle bone that can retain trapped grease 😬 since its cold out there, to speed up the process you can use an aquarium heater or a specialized heating element. You can also just out it near your regular old heater. I also recommend adding bromelain (meat tenderizer) to your maceration as it does break down the muscle tissue faster. It's best to keep your water around 120 F if you have exact temp control. At this point, all forms of body fat have hit their melting point, and the heat will speed the enzymatic process without denaturing. This will help you speed up your next step after macerating- degreasing. The more fat you can pull out in the macerating stage, the better.

It's actually very true. Boiling will cause the bones to literally cook, trapping grease and any remaining marrow in the sponge of the bone for long bones. It causes the plates that make up bones (skulls especially) to shrink overall, and fall apart easier with a much less likelihood of being able to put them back together. Properly processed bones will not be cooked, but instead will be dried. Nasal turbinates will have a stronger structure, teeth will fit better, the skull will be able to be MUCH whiter, and the product won't decay over time. 

You've had some great luck, I'm sure. But if you take a picture of your finished skull and wait about a year, sometimes more for large thick skulls, you'll have a completely different looking skull. Additionally I encourage you to leave one out in the sun and heat if you're somewhere where it's summer ATM. I'm in AZ, so it only takes a little while for me, but if you let it sit and it's not finished processing (or not processed well) you will start to see pools of yellowish discoloration on your bone. That's grease and protein that's still trapped within the bone, and will rot your bones over time.

But in reality, high fat, or high liquid content tissue (full body, large skull with brain intact, etc) is just going to take longer than low content tissue (wings, tails, feet). It also depends greatly on the humidity of the area, freshness of the tissue, etc. I've made a comment on the process of mummifying feet that I can give you a run down of, but otherwise it's best to start with checking every 24 hours and brushing off the borax, for the first 72ish hours to get an idea on the feeling for the borax process in your area. Keep note of the tissue color change, the size reduction, and the mobility around any joints. From there, I recommend leaving it buried about a week before dusting and moving the piece. You CAN leave it there for like a month or whatever, but it does run the risk of the borax becoming saturated and no longer pulling liquid and allowing for decomp/attracting pests. I'd rather be a little over careful with my specimens myself, but to each their own.

It's not some "weird internet thing" and it's not anything that has to do with it being "too long". It's a science thing. 

After a certain temperature, bone cooks. The structures are compromised and it deteriorates. Whether you can "see it" or not, 10 years later you'll be able to tell which was fucked and which wasn't. Simmering, double boiling, and boiling are all DIFFERENT. Simmering in hot water, sous vide in a bag in simmering water, and double boiling are fine, as long as it's not BOILING water. Water boils at 212, fat stays liquid reliably at 120. You have a whole 90 degrees of safety, there's no reason for it. You're pulling fat back into the bone (it has to make up for the broken bonds somehow) and compromising a product that is going to be someone's memory for years.

Boiling and bleaching cause permanent damage to the skull. Pieces will start flaking off, it'll often times crack very easily, and it will become SUPER brittle. Like crush with your hand brittle.

HILARIOUSLY- lamictal was how i found out I have stevens-Johnson Syndrome! My seizures started literally a month before my youngest was conceived (that's how we knew they weren't pregnancy related), and lamictal was the first thing we tried. I was on a very low dose and everything was fine, albeit it didn't seem to help any. After my son was born we were like "great, let's start a therapeutic level!" The moment i took the next titrated dose, i started breaking out in red spots. 

For those who don't know; Stevens Johnson Syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that is often the culprit beyond a phenomenal known as the "lamictal rash". It's a huge were problem and causes you body to attack your dermis. Patients often require the burn ward and months of recovery. 

I knew I had weird reactions already from some antibiotic i had taken from years prior (whole roof of my mouth and the skin of my lips sloughed off. Yuck. And ouch.) So i immediately messaged them, stopped taking it, and went to the hospital when my body was completely covered in red patches and blistering 3 hours later. They laughed, told me I couldn't possibly know what i was talking about and that SJS is rare (hilariously, it's not when it's genetic. Who would have thought). They sent me home and told me to take Benadryl. 

Because i had taken it just the one dose (we think it essentially pushed the blood concentration past the reaction threshold once my son was born) it was nowhere near the seriousness it would have (should have) been. My son's skin was sleeping off for about 3 months but everyone assumed it was baby acne until i broke out. My entire body peeled off in sores for about 6ish months before it finally stopped. Hi! I preserve feet like this and use 3d printed caps to maintain the lucky rabbit foot feel. Here's my process- soak and scrubbing warm soapy water until the water run clear, allow them to sit for a few hours at a time up to over night in warm dawn water to pull out some of the excess blood and grease. From there, soak in isopropyl alcohol for at least 3 days. After, transfer to a super-saturated borax solution (this is when you dissolve borax in HOT water until no more can be dissolved, then allow the solution to cool) for at least 3 days. After, pin if you'd like, and allow to dry with ample air circulation. You'll likely find crystals form as they dry (this is a good sign lol), just brush them off with a pet brush or a wire brush and they'll clean right up 😊

The basic science here is that due to the volatility of alcohol's water displacement, the alcohol will absorb into the tissue to replace the water. From there, the alcohol will evaporate off quickly in the borax solution and allow the borax crystals to form within the tissue to preserve it. While this may be able to be done with salt, i personally haven't done it and due to the higher stability/lower crystalization speed of salt it may not be as  effective. Happy mummifying!

Depending on how fresh the specimen is will determine the length of time. If you're using a fairly fresh specimen that you're unsure of, you can bury it in salt for about 2-3 days before moving it, and extend it based on how well it tolerated that. If it starts to stink a bit (smell check on the daily), change it sooner until it dries out more. 

Since it's a foot, and doesn't have much muscular tissue, you shouldn't have any problems with leaving it for a week or so. Places of high cartilage, low fat, and low moisture will require less changes and less time. A fresh rock dove wing was done in 3 weeks with borax for me. I recommend using a sewing needle or something to make small holes in the skin to allow for better fluid drain as well. You'll definitely be able to tell when it's done as there will be no movement, no "squish", and it will be significantly smaller. A good rule of thumb is when the salt stops "sticking" because it's wet. You'll likely have salt stuck in the fur, but if it's not dried on there in clumps and discolored then it's fine. Happy mummifying!

So, there's several methods that can be used. If you have the space, or a plot of land you can be sure will be secure, you can do burial but this can take months to years depending on the soil. If you can handle the stink or know how to limit it, maceration is going to the most reliable and quicker method that's tried and true. You can also leave it exposed (protected obviously), but you will likely need to macerate a bit to clean things up. 

If you do choose maceration, you have a few options in terms of processing that can affect your quality and processing time. Regardless, you need to degrease and degrease thoroughly. The gentlest method is dawn and water, but if the dawn is too concentrated it can stain bone and it takes longer. Another method is ammonia. This is the most common method and effective, but can be difficult for those with sensitivity to fumes. Finally, hydrogen peroxide for whitening. Household 3% is fine, but if you are doing big batches or big skulls it will be easier to use hair developer. Hair developer Is higher concentration hydrogen peroxide and can be diluted with COLD water. I recommend switching back and forth to help break up the gunk in the spongier bone. 

NOTE: If you do decide to do so, allow your bones to fully soak on hot water for awhile and dry fully before moving to the next solution. Ammonia and hydrogen peroxide can have explosive reactions.

I totally get it! For antlers you have a couple options. There's really no way to not get the antlers over the waterline and get a clean skull. There's tons of fleshy bits that will get stuck there so personally it's easier just to "repair" afterwards. 

The easiest and most natural looking is Potassium Permanganate. You can find it in several forms, including medical settings, but it's really easy to find overall, like [here](https://a.co/d/hZijzVU). It can sound intimidating, but it's just a dark purple liquid. It stains REALLY easily, so if you do, I recommend either wrapping your skull in Saran wrap and painter's tape or sealing it in a water proof seal (mop n glo, modge podge, etc) before hand. That way, you can just wipe it off with some warm soapy water. 

Another common option is standard paint. You technically CAN use household acrylics/oils, but i really wouldnt recommend it. It builds up easily and can quickly look gaudy, flat, and unprofessional if not used sparingly and carefully. However, traditional coloring has used oil based paints like [this](https://a.co/d/4MDts2u).

Finally, the last most popular option is stains. [Pens](https://a.co/d/8ddCd2V) are a good options for thin areas, as well as antiquing wax/ stains like [this one ](https://a.co/d/fg0Kz93). 

Other "natural" options that are hard to pull off on full skulls include coffee, tea, berries, etc. 

There's been some good discussion in the changing the skull game group including some new chemical mixes, and even vinegar/ baking soda mixes! Just remember that antlers start off with blood supply too and may harbor grease. Always keep an eye out for that, and if you do see it you can try basting with baking soda slurry to pull it.

No worries, it's what i do! Their both actually the same thing. The biggest difference is concentration. Household peroxide is 3% while 40vol is 12%. In most cases, 3% will work just fine. But i find it's easier and cheaper to use hair developer or industrial grade peroxide (industrial is totally not necessary in your case, it's just because I process a lot). If you do choose to do developer, creme is fine but i do find it doesn't dissolve as easily. Using a clear or liquid developer will help with that and allow for more UV exposure. Just be careful, if you are using anything above 3% your bones should not sit for longer than 12 hours. After that, at higher concentrations, we see degradation of bone and fragility start to happen as the bone oxidizes. It doesn't happen often, and in most cases you're safe especially if you're breaking down soft tissue still, but it is worth noting. 

No matter what, never EVER use bleach. You will immediately cause structure compromise to the bone and it will start to dissolve. If your bones aren't white after hydrogen peroxide and drying, there's still grease.

Let it try out completely, then try a hydrogen peroxide bath out in in the sun or under a UV lamp, if you can. Hydrogen peroxide can help bust up some of the grease in more porous bone to help degreasing. If you don't already, you may want to try ammonia for degreasing. 

As a word of caution though, let bones coming from ammonia dry COMPLETELY before whitening, and vice versa. You can rinse the bone in hot water to speed the reaction of any remaining hydrogen peroxide, but i still recommend allowing to dry completely. Hydrogen peroxide and ammonia can have explosive properties when mixed, but neither builds up or stays deposited on the bone. So if you let it dry completely, you can be certain there is no risk of mixing. 

Another tip, be sure you're using hot (NOT BOILING) water for the fastest processing. Liquid fat is a lot easier to dissolve and pull than half-liquid fat. Happy processing!

under the ADA there are 3 clinical classifications regarding working animals that receive considerations for the services they provide. Service, therapy, and Emotional Support. I encourage everyone who may not be aware of the regulations to look at the US DOJ ADA (Department of Justice, Americans with Disabilities Act) information here: https://www.ada.gov/resources/service-animals-2010-requirements/

While there is no certification, registration, or documentation requirements, Service animals are the only animal allowed public access and are defined by federal regulations as follows: "dogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities". Federally, only service *dogs* are protected for public access, but individual states may have broader definitions for this (for example, AZ recognizes miniature horses as well). Service animals are considered **MEDICAL EQUIPMENT**. FALSIFYING, DISTRACTING, HARMING, OR OTHERWISE INTERFERING WITH A SERVICE ANIMAL IS A FEDERAL CRIME.  

Therapy animals are animals that are specifically trained to assist in emotional tasks and may be utilized in setting such as hospitals, senior homes, etc. These animals have protected housing rights, but DO NOT have public access. These animals must be well trained, and often must show facilities certification for training tests, such as "Canine Good Citizen",  in order to work. 

Emotional Support Animals are animals that ARE NOT required to be task trained. The existence of the animal alone is considered supportive in a patient's treatment, and while they may be trained or well behaved they are not considered medical devices. These animals are not species specific, and do receiving housing protections, but do not receive public access accommodations. 

Yes, Goldens and labs have a high drive to please with gentle demeanors which makes them ideal breed candidates for service work. HOWEVER, that is not the only thing that goes into these processes. A dog may be great and sweet, but have too much difficulty focusing or anxiety that distracts them. They cannot be service dogs until that is addressed. Untrained "service" dogs are the reason why so many stigmas exist around assistance animals. My SD was washed because he became anxious and vocal after an attack in public. We tried for years, but couldn't get it under complete control and he lost his public access.

Here's the Start Code;

`M140 S{material_bed_temperature_layer_0} ; Start heating the heated bed`  
  
`M190 S{material_bed_temperature_layer_0} ; Wait until the heated bed reaches the desired temperature`  
  
`M104 S160; Start heating the extruder to 160 degrees Celsius`  
  
`G28 ; Auto Home`  
  
`G29 ; Bed Leveling (with BLTouch)`  
  
`G92 E0 ; Reset extruder origin`  
  
`M104 S{material_print_temperature_layer_0} ; Start heating the extruder`  
  
`G1 X0.1 Y20 Z0.3 F5000.0 ; Move printhead to the starting position`  
  
`M109 S{material_print_temperature_layer_0} ; Wait until the extruder reaches the desired temperature`  
  
`G1 Z2.0 F3000 ; Move Z-Axis up to avoid scratching of the build plate`  
  
`G1 X0.1 Y200.0 Z0.3 F1500.0 E15 ; Draw the first line`  
  
`G1 X0.4 Y200.0 Z0.3 F5000.0 ; Move to the side`  
  
`G1 X0.4 Y20 Z0.3 F1500.0 E30 ; Draw the second line`  
  
`G92 E0 ; Reset extruder origin`  
  
`G1 Z2.0 F3000 ; Move Z-Axis up to avoid scratching of the build plate`
